blocks: Recently a novel gene on human chromosome 1, Cancer Associated Ring-1 (CAR-1) of the RBCC subfamily, was identified as a candidate tumor suppressor gene. Members of the RBCC family have been observed to form macromolecular structures that may be crucial for the normal function of these proteins. In this study, the CAR-1 protein was characterized through Western blots, immunocytochemistry, and immunohistochemistry on normal and tumor samples. The Western blot indicated that CAR-1 is a 64 kD protein. Immunocytochemistry analysis of normal tissues yielded a diffuse background staining for the CAR-1 protein that included speckling, similar to the macromolecular structures of BRCA1 and other RING finger proteins. In contrast, in tumors, CAR-1 displayed a distinct spider-like network of staining but without the numerous speckles found in the normal cells. Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed CAR-1 staining in only very specific cells, particularly around the ductal structures as seen in breast, uterus, and kidney tissue samples.

The advent of cancer and the metastasis thereof is a convoluted pathway involving a spectrum of changes to the genome of a normal cell that include of point mutations, gene amplification, recombination, gene deletion, reduced or overexpression, and loss of heterozygosity (LOH). Many of these targeted genes have been singled out as oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.¹ Tumor suppressor genes code for proteins that function in the cell cycle to suppress or inhibit the growth of tumor cells by inhibiting cell proliferation. Without their normal and active presence, the genesis of tumors or the preclusion of apoptosis can occur. In cancer cells, tumor suppressor genes can be deleted, mutated, methylated, or their expression downregulated.¹,²

The isolation of a particular tumor suppressor gene involves a series of steps, narrowing the region of location and discovering the extent and mechanism of its inactivation in cancer. Mapping of genomic loss of heterozygosity (LOH) should show sites of LOH of alleles on a chromosome that suggest the inactivation of a tumor suppressor gene at that site for a specific tumor.³ Evidence must also prove that the suspected tumor suppressor gene has suffered loss of expression or is considerably downregulated in the same cancer form where LOH was detected. Mutational screenings

and methylation tests further establish tumor suppressor gene inactivation. Gene expression is determined through functional studies involving the tumor suppressor gene protein that will suggest the function and localization of that protein. Cells transfected with the candidate tumor suppressor gene are injected into mice with malignancies. The results will confirm whether or not introduction of the gene into a malignancy that contains the inactive gene significantly suppresses the tumor.

The Ring-B-box-Coiled-coil domain (RBCC) proteins, a subfamily of the RING finger protein family, are suspected interactors in tumorigenesis through gene expression regulation, cellular proliferation, oncogenesis, apoptosis, and ubiquitination.⁴⁻⁸ Through a functional genetic approach with suppression subtractive hybridization cloning, a novel member of the RBCC subfamily has been identified as CAR-1 (Cancer Associated Ring-1) and its full-length cDNA isolated. The proposed structure of the CAR-1 protein consists of an RBCC domain followed by an rfp domain, which has been shown to function as a transcriptional repressor and to be a protein that interacts in cellular epigenetic silencing mechanisms (Fig. 1).

CAR-1 has been mapped to a chromosomal region where high frequency loss of heterozygosity has been shown in breast, colon, and brain cancers. This region also shares proximity with a translocation breakpoint region in a renal carcinoma cell line.
